name: Bimaxillary osteotomy (bimax)

lead: Bimaxillary osteotomy, or bimax, is an operation in which a surgeon cuts both the upper jaw (maxilla) and lower jaw (mandible) through the mouth, moves them to a new position and fixes them with plates and screws. Clinically it is used for bite problems such as underbites and overbites, jaw-joint problems and obstructive sleep apnoea, and in looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as the route to a stronger profile and jawline, often with counter-clockwise rotation of the jaws.

Bone cuts allow the maxilla (typically a Le Fort I osteotomy) and mandible (typically a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy) to be moved forward, back, up, down or rotated. Published research supports it for bite and airway outcomes and reports high patient satisfaction with appearance; formal evidence on purely cosmetic results is limited.

paras: Braces usually align the teeth for months before surgery and again afterward, and 3D virtual planning is increasingly used to plan the movements. Surgery is performed under general anaesthesia by an oral and maxillofacial surgeon, followed by months of recovery.

Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection, temporary or permanent numbness of the lip and chin, temporomandibular joint problems, condylar resorption, relapse of the jaw position and months of recovery and orthodontics. It is regulated as ordinary surgery in most countries, and cosmetic-only indications are judged case by case by surgeons.

angle.text: Bimax repositions both jaws, changing facial proportions, bite and airway, with visible skeletal change after healing. The operation is established for bite and airway problems; the cosmetic results forums describe vary by case.

lead: Bimaxillary osteotomy, commonly called bimax, double-jaw surgery or two-jaw surgery, is a form of orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery in which both the upper jaw (maxilla) and the lower jaw (mandible) are cut, moved to a new position and fixed with plates and screws, usually through incisions inside the mouth.[1][1] For appearance, it is the operation that lets a surgeon change the position of the whole lower face at once: bringing a recessed midface and chin forward, setting back a protruding jaw, correcting asymmetry or a gummy smile, and rotating the jaws to change the profile. It is also used for bite discrepancies, jaw-joint problems and obstructive sleep apnoea.[1]

The operation grew out of 19th- and 20th-century jaw surgery, with Simon P. Hullihen's 1849 case and Hugo Obwegeser's mid-century work on the upper and lower jaw usually cited in its history.[1][1][2] In modern practice a team of oral and maxillofacial surgeons and orthodontists plans the movements with X-rays, photographs and 3D software, and braces or aligners usually align the teeth before and after surgery.[1][1][3]

Published research on the procedure mostly examines planning methods, anaesthesia, pain control, blood loss, joint effects and quality of life, with some studies of facial soft-tissue change and patient satisfaction.[4][5][6][7][8][9] One review of bimaxillary osteotomy for sleep apnoea reports sustained improvements in breathing measures and that many patients also describe a positive change in facial aesthetics, alongside sensory disturbance and temporary jaw restriction. Documented longer-term concerns include condylar resorption and relapse.[10][11][12]

On forums such as looksmax.org, bimax is discussed as the biggest structural option in the facial-surgery toolkit, alongside Le Fort I advancement, genioplasty, braces, implants and rhinoplasty, with recurring questions about counter-clockwise rotation, insurance coverage, orthodontic preparation and travelling abroad for surgery.[13][14]

paras: In a bimaxillary osteotomy the maxilla and mandible are each divided by controlled bone cuts so that they can be moved as separate units and then stabilised with titanium plates and screws.[1] Orthognathic surgery in general is done to correct jaw mismatches in the front-to-back, vertical or side-to-side direction and can be used for airway, joint and aesthetic goals.[1]

The upper-jaw cut is usually a Le Fort I osteotomy and the lower-jaw cut is usually a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy; a chin procedure (genioplasty) may be added.[1] Combined upper and lower jaw advancement for sleep apnoea is also called maxillomandibular advancement.

Orthognathic surgery can move the jaws forward, back, up, down or sideways, and rotate them as a unit. Surgeons describe the upper-jaw component as a Le Fort I osteotomy, a name borrowed from the facial-fracture lines described by the French surgeon René Le Fort, and the lower-jaw component most often as a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO), which splits each side of the mandible lengthwise so the tooth-bearing segment can slide.[1][2] Additional options include genioplasty (moving the chin), rapid palatal expansion for a narrow upper jaw, and newer techniques such as custom implants listed in overviews of the field.[1]

When both jaws are advanced the operation is also called maxillomandibular advancement (MMA). It has been used for obstructive sleep apnoea since the late 1970s, after advancing the lower jaw was noticed to improve sleepiness in a small number of patients, and is typically considered after other airway surgeries, according to a general encyclopedia account.[15]

One of the first published jaw-correction cases was reported by Simon P. Hullihen in 1849.[1][1] Jaw osteotomies became established in the 1940s and after, and the Austrian-trained surgeon Hugo Obwegeser (1920-2017), who trained under Richard Trauner at Graz and is often called a father of modern orthognathic surgery, popularised the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy and developed the modern Le Fort I osteotomy.[1][2] He presented his techniques to North American surgeons in 1966 and described combining upper and lower jaw surgery in one operation in about 1969-1970.[2]

Rigid fixation with titanium plates in the following decades reduced the need to wire the jaws shut for weeks, and 3D imaging and computer-aided planning spread from the 1990s onward.[1] In 2002 a surgeon named Raffaini was reported to have introduced the operation under local anaesthesia with intravenous sedation, allowing faster recovery without a hospital stay.[1] Meta-analyses in the 2020s compare virtual with traditional planning, and reviews examine how accurately 3D software predicts soft-tissue change.[4][3]

Surgeons plan jaw movements around bite, airway and facial balance. Reviews of 3D soft-tissue simulation report mean prediction errors across the whole face from about 0.27 mm to 2.9 mm, with the largest errors after bimaxillary surgery (with or without genioplasty) reported in regions that move with the underlying bone and lips.[3] That body of work is the technical basis for before-and-after previews shown to patients.

In forum language, planned movements are often described by their rotation: counter-clockwise rotation (CCW) means the jaws pivot so the chin and lower face move forward and up, shortening the lower third and changing the profile. A looksmax.org reply in a thread on double-jaw surgery describes it as a Le Fort plus BSSO moved counter-clockwise.[16] Members also describe goals of facial masculinisation, a stronger jawline in profile, correcting a recessed maxilla seen as under-eye hollowing, and fixing mouth breathing or a gummy smile; a poster considering surgery in Poland states a goal of aesthetic improvement and masculinisation, not just medical correction.[14][16]

Costs vary widely by country and surgeon, and forum answers to price questions are typically that it depends on the surgeon.[13] Forum threads on insurance describe coverage as depending on a documented functional problem such as an underbite, and posters share what they say was covered; a thread titled around insurance coverage carries a disclaimer from its author.[17] Posters also compare clinics abroad, for example surgeons in Poland, and ask for before-and-after photos and aesthetic track records.[14] Coverage rules and prices are set by individual insurers, health systems and clinics, and are not covered by the clinical literature.[1]

A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 cohort studies with 1,482 participants examined which factors influence oral-health-related quality of life after orthognathic surgery, using the Orthognathic Quality of Life Questionnaire-22 and the Oral Health Impact Profile-14, with subgroup comparisons by country development level, type of deformity, type of procedure and sex.[9] Its starting premise is that orthognathic surgery improves both oral function and appearance for patients with dentofacial disharmony.[9]

An earlier survey study asked which variables affect patients' perceived improvement and satisfaction after orthognathic surgery.[8] A review on the duration of orthognathic-surgical treatment has also looked at how long the combined orthodontic and surgical pathway takes.[18]

Planning typically involves a team of oral and maxillofacial surgeons and orthodontists, with X-rays, photographs and 3D software used to predict the result.[1] Orthodontic preparation has traditionally taken up to a year, and newer approaches include surgery-first protocols and clear aligners.[1] Users on looksmax.org report that braces generally stay on through surgery and that orthodontic treatment is needed before and after a bimaxillary operation.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of virtual versus traditional surgical planning in bimaxillary osteotomy found that virtual planning shortened planning time significantly, while the difference in time spent in the operating room was not significant.[4] A 2025 retrospective study introduced a coefficient for measuring how closely bimaxillary advancement matches its virtual plan.

General descriptions of orthognathic surgery say initial healing takes around two to six weeks, with complete bone healing taking a further two to four months, a mostly liquid or soft diet at first and swelling that can persist for weeks to months.[1] Older techniques wired the jaws shut for several weeks, while modern practice typically uses rigid fixation and avoids prolonged wiring.[1]

Human research on bimaxillary osteotomy is largely about technique and perioperative care. A systematic review concluded that deliberate hypotensive anaesthesia reduced blood loss, with serious organ-hypoperfusion consequences reported as uncommon.[5] Randomised trials have examined intravenous ibuprofen for preventive analgesia in patients planned for bimaxillary osteotomy and tranexamic acid for blood loss in orthognathic surgery.[6]

A systematic review of 76 studies covering about 3,400 patients examined the effect of orthognathic surgery on the temporomandibular joint and oral function; the authors reported that variation in techniques, examination methods and study design made conclusions difficult. Older clinical series of Le Fort I and bimaxillary osteotomies in patients with open bite documented condylar remodelling and resorption, and a long-term evaluation described progressive condylar resorption after orthognathic surgery.[10][11]

A three-dimensional study of 44 patients, including 20 Class III patients treated by bimaxillary osteotomy, measured facial soft-tissue asymmetry before and up to six months after surgery.[7] A survey study examined which variables influence patients' perceived improvement and satisfaction after orthognathic surgery.[8] For sleep apnoea, a recent review reports improvements in apnoea-hypopnoea index, blood pressure and sleep architecture after bimaxillary osteotomy.

A 2021 overview of five systematic reviews covering 5,128 patients reported condylar resorption in 12.32% of patients across orthognathic procedures, with 70.1% of the affected patients having had double-jaw surgery; the authors said bimaxillary surgery could be considered a risk factor but cautioned that deformity type, movement type and fixation also influence the result.[12] The large 1998 series of 259 open-bite patients, all with Le Fort I osteotomy and 117 also with sagittal split advancement, examined joint sounds and condylar remodelling and resorption.[10]

Recent randomised trials on recovery include a double-blind trial of single-dose intravenous dexketoprofen for pain and swelling in Class III patients undergoing double-jaw surgery, a 48-patient trial of adding ropivacaine before extubation after bimaxillary osteotomy, and a trial of ultrasound-guided maxillary and mandibular nerve blocks and morphine consumption after double-jaw surgery.[19][20][21] A registered trial of augmented reality for patient education in orthognathic surgery enrolled 60 participants.[22] A case report and review has described double-jaw surgery in a patient with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a group of conditions historically considered to complicate elective surgery because of bleeding, healing and joint concerns.[23]

Common reported adverse effects of orthognathic surgery include bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea and numbness caused by injury to the inferior alveolar nerve, which usually recovers over about three months, with permanent numbness described as rare.[1] A review of bimaxillary osteotomy for sleep apnoea lists temporary or permanent sensory disorders, a temporary reduction in oral-health quality of life and temporarily restricted lower-jaw function.

Jaw-joint effects, condylar resorption and relapse of the jaw position are documented longer-term concerns.[10][11] Planning descriptions also mention psychological assessment to confirm that surgery is appropriate and to anticipate its effects.[1]

Surgeons' overviews list infection (reported at up to about 7% in one overview, with perioperative antibiotics reducing it), swelling, bleeding, nausea and nerve-related numbness, and describe maxillary impaction as among the riskier movements.[1] A 1995 study of 83 patients linked removing third molars during the same operation to higher rates of hardware infection.[1] Recovery guidance in surgeons' overviews mentions a liquid diet with common weight loss, pain medication for about 6-8 days, return to work after about 2-6 weeks and activity restrictions for about 8 weeks.[1]

Forum members describe bimax as a bigger structural change than implants or chin surgery, and posts about it often cover counter-clockwise rotation, orthodontic requirements, insurance and travelling to another country for surgery. Discussion of cost coverage frequently cites bite problems such as an underbite as the route to insurance funding, though policies differ by country and insurer.

Forum threads cover choosing between single-jaw and double-jaw options for retrognathia, whether jaw surgery makes sense for a rounded jawline, results galleries and what orthodontists advise; one thread records a user whose orthodontist advised against double-jaw surgery and asks follow-up questions.[24] Teenagers also post asking whether they should have surgery at 18 for a recessed midface, and replies discuss whether facial structure will change with puberty.[16]

Related interventions include Le Fort I advancement alone, genioplasty, facial implants, rhinoplasty, orthodontic camouflage and non-surgical approaches such as mewing and myofunctional therapy that forums discuss for the same facial-structure goals; surgery-first protocols and clear aligners are newer orthodontic variants within orthognathic care.[1][1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, bimax is discussed as a major hard-tissue procedure, often in combination with other surgeries, with threads on insurance, braces and operating abroad.

claims.claim: Bimax can be covered by insurance if there is a functional bite problem such as an underbite.
Braces are needed before and after bimax, and stay on during the operation.
Bimax with counter-clockwise rotation gives a better-looking profile than the same patient's current appearance suggests.
Bimax improves overall facial harmony and the airway at the same time.
Double-jaw surgery is a major route to 'ascending' because it changes the whole facial skeleton.
A recessed maxilla and bad profile can be fixed by moving the jaws forward.
Condylar resorption and relapse are rare.
Surgery abroad is a way to get a better aesthetic result or lower cost.

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known jaw-correction cases.[1][1]
Jaw osteotomies become established surgical techniques.[1]
Hugo Obwegeser, with Trauner, is credited with the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy that underpins modern lower-jaw surgery.
Obwegeser presents his orthognathic techniques to North American surgeons in Washington, DC.[2]
Obwegeser describes combining Le Fort I and sagittal split osteotomies in one bimaxillary operation.[2]
Jaw advancement is noted to improve sleepiness and begins to be used for sleep apnoea.[15]
Rigid titanium plate fixation reduces the need for prolonged jaw immobilisation.
3D imaging and computer-aided planning spread through orthognathic practice.
A 259-patient clinical and radiological study documents condylar remodelling and resorption after Le Fort I and bimaxillary osteotomies.[10]
Raffaini reported to have introduced the operation under local anaesthesia with sedation.[1]
An overview of five systematic reviews reports condylar resorption in 12.32% of 5,128 patients.[12]
A meta-analysis reports shorter planning time with virtual planning in bimaxillary osteotomy.[4]
A meta-analysis of 22 cohort studies examines quality-of-life outcomes after orthognathic surgery.[9]
